title: Tiny Expect With Two Matchers
statement:
Write a tiny version of the expect function from test runners like Jest. expect(val) returns an object with two methods:

  • toBe(other) returns true if val === other. Otherwise it throws an error with the message "Not Equal".
  • notToBe(other) returns true if val !== other. Otherwise it throws an error with the message "Equal".

The harness cannot call methods or catch errors itself, so the tested entry point is runMatcher(val, matcher, other). It calls expect(val)[matcher](other), where matcher is "toBe" or "notToBe". It returns "pass" if the matcher returned true, or the thrown error's message if it threw.

Values are numbers (integers), strings, booleans or null. Equality is strict: different types are never equal, so 1 is not "1" and not true.

examples.why: A number and a string are never strictly equal, even if they print the same.
null === null, so notToBe throws with the message "Equal".

constraints: val and other are integers, strings, booleans or null
hints: expect(val) has to return something that still knows val later, when toBe is called. What JavaScript feature does that?
Return an object literal whose methods close over val.
Each method compares with ===. On failure, throw new Error("Not Equal") or new Error("Equal"). The entry point wraps the call in try/catch and returns err.message.

explain.intuition:
expect(val) is called once, and its methods are called later. They still need val, so they close over it: the object literal's methods capture the parameter of expect. That is the whole trick behind fluent assertion APIs like expect(x).toBe(y).

Failure is reported by throwing, not by returning false. Test runners catch the error and use its message in the report, which is why the message text matters. Comparison uses ===, which never converts types: 1 == "1" is true, but 1 === "1" is false.
steps: toBe: if val !== other, throw new Error("Not Equal"); else return true.
notToBe: if val === other, throw new Error("Equal"); else return true.
runMatcher: call the matcher inside try; return "pass", or err.message in catch.
pitfalls: Using ==. It treats 0, "" and false as equal, and null == undefined.
Throwing a plain string instead of an Error. Then err.message is undefined.
In Python, comparing with == alone: 1 == True is true there. Check the types as well.

solutions.title: Closure returning an object
solutions.idea: The matcher methods close over val, compare strictly, and throw an Error with the required message on failure.

followups: Add toEqual, which compares arrays and plain objects by content instead of by reference.
Add a .not property so expect(x).not.toBe(y) works for every matcher without writing each one twice.
lcTitle: To Be Or Not To Be
